   PLEASE SEND YOUR TEXTFILE!
Text is accepted in any form for
OUTLETTERS: wordprocessor files
(say which),typed or handwritten
letters. However, PLEASE send us
a textfile if possible so your
letter needn't be typed again!
The easiest for us to edit are
Tasword 2 files with the right
margin set at 32 but a textfile
in ANY format is appreciated!

Please state if there should be
parts of your letter you do not
wish published but we always use
our discretion anyway. Letters
may also be edited for clarity
and length... Please ask if you
welcome direct correspondence
from other OUTLET readers and we
will publish your full address.

From Kevin Gould, LINCS.

I have recently been given a
copy of TogMod written by Brian
Gaff as I am hoping this will
answer a problem I have got. I
currently use a Spectrum +2A,+D,
3.5" disc drive and the +2a's
printer port as my Commodore ink
jet printer has a 36-pin Centr-
onics parallel printer connector
as does the +2a.

I currently have to use software
such as Tasword 2 in 128K mode
which is fine. However, it would
be nice to have the option of
using the 48K mode as well as
the printer port. Togmod seems
the ideal answer but I can't
figure out how it works.


Brian Cavers to Kevin Gould

You don't say but we reckon you
must be using a FIXIT etc. to
get your +D working on a +2a.It
is likely that the Togmod rout-
ine may clash with the +D in
that situation and it may not be
possible to resolve it.

In any event, Togmod will only
work on entering the listing -
it will not switch modes in a
running program. Nobody has yet
found a way to switch modes in a
running program I don't think.

You might try ROUTE 48 (OUTLET
31) which can switch to 48K in a
running program but not back to
128K!                 Brian

From Chris Oliver, STAFFS

 Re: MUSIFILE 2 in ADDENDERS in
     answer to Jim Hossack.

Thanks Jim Hossack, for sending
in a corrected version of your
"MUSIFILE". Yes, it is better to
modify the published version of
a program, if you notice bugs
have crept in, and send that
rather than a complex list of
"Change line xxxx to zzz etc.".

Alternatively, one could submit
a "Patch" program of just a few
lines to Merge into the original
to replace the faulty lines.

In response to some of your
comments:-


a).The BOLD char-set which is
usually called by GOSUB 9994: A
pity that there is not enough
space left in memory to include
this, but instead of resetting
the machine as you suggested,
one can recall the normal sparse
Sinclair set by POKEing system-
variable "CHARS" at 23606/7 with
its default values of 0 & 60.
I've now included this in the
initialisation in line 8810, in
case the OUTLET set had been
called by a previous program.


b).The POKE with zero in line
220 is something which has
caught me out before now,
especially when looking at a
printed listing of a program.


The problem arises when one uses
the command "RUN" which clears
the variables area of RAM so the
Spectrum no longer knows what
letter "O" represents.

We use "O" in OUTLET programs
instead of zero to save bytes: A
single letter variable takes up
only one byte whereas a Spectrum
stores numbers (including zero)
in Basic in a minimum of seven
bytes, ie,first its character(s)
then the byte 14 which indicates
it is a numerical value followed
by the 5-byte representation of
the number. If you want to know
more about how numbers are
stored in the Spectrum, see
FAMOUS 5 in OUTLET issue 32.
                           Chris


From Ron Cavers



I am writing in response to the
OUTWORK entry from Francis Miles
regarding his project to produce
a spreadsheet for the Spectrum.


   [see new OUTWORK section
   later in this issue - BC]


As my "day" job involves the
regular use of spreadsheets on
an Altos 5000 running under Unix
- plus I have also used them on
the SAM, Spectrum and a PC - I
thought I would jot down my own
musings on the subject...


1). The vast majority of spread-
sheet files are simple affairs
and this would be even more true
on the domestic front (via the
Spectrum) so my own recommend-
ation would be not to sacrifice
program strengths just to make
available more memory than 99%
of users would ever use.

2). Printer interfacing is a
major problem so either the
BASIC should be accessible or
comprehensive user options
available in the program.

3). Each cell contains text,
data or a formula and I have
encountered endless frustrations
with some spreadsheets when
inputting this information.


The program needs to know what
the input is, of course, and my
suggestions would be for the =
(equals) key to indicate a
formula to be entered, any
number or numeric operand would
indicate data input with all
else being text.


All types of input can then be
decided from the first keypress
- except in cases of mixed
alpha/numeric (e.g. Serial Nos.
of the form 12 H 45 JKL etc) in
which case an override key is
needed to define a text input
(perhaps TRUE VIDEO or some
other rarely used shift key on
the Spectrum), but also see note
5).


4). The other type of entry
(which, I think, is generally
classed as data) is calendar
dates and, as these can be quite
crucial in some spreadsheet
files, some thought needs to be
given on how the program is to
handle them. As I mentioned in a
recent letter in OUTLET, most
spreadsheets use the convention
of storing dates as the number a
days since 31st December 1899,
i.e 1st January 1900 = day 1.
However, the actual on-screen
presentation needs some thought
as my favourite (16 Jan 93
rather than 16th Jan '93) still
takes up more visual space than
is often required. Some shift
key to toggle particular cell
displays, say to 16 Jan?


- And what happens in the year
2000? 16 Jan 00 looks a bit odd
but what's the alternative! Some
thought is also needed on input-
ting dates as, following my own
suggestions, attempting to input
16.1.93 would fool the program
into treating it as normal data
(and crash at the second decimal
point) or refuse to accept the
input and leave a user scratch-
ing his/her head as to why a
logical input was refused. The
program I use accepts 16/1/93
and converts it to a number(but,
annoyingly, about 6 further key-
presses are then required to
display the number as a recog-
nisable date). Ideally inputting
16/1/93 should store it as a
number(say 34567)but immediately
present it as 16 Jan (say).

5). I usually find that my
spreadsheet input is in batches
e.g. blocks of text, then data
and dates. I have therefore
speculated on the usefulness of
a shift key that would toggle
through the following options:


DATA/TEXT/DATE/INTERPRET

The first 3 options would define
the type of entry (with possible
crashes when the user forgets
and types text whilst in data
mode!) with the last option
allowing the program to
interpret your input as in 3).
above. I still wonder if this
would cause more trouble than
not.


6). No, my mouth's running away
with my fingers so I'm calling a
halt for now.

I hope some of these musing are
useful - just wind me up and set
me running if you want any more!

                         Ron

From M.D. Atkins, BURY




Ron & Brian


Thank you for your reply to my
query on TABLOID[OUTLETTERS 73].


First of all, you have answered
the question that I asked and
also one that I didn't ask i.e.
that the command is not in the
BASIC program. However, the
questions I should have asked
are (i) Why isn't the command in
the BASIC part of the program,
and (ii) How is it called?


I'm sorry I did not make this
clear. The problem arose when I
examined the "Contents" program
to see what printer commands
were used and I could not find
the ESC 3 n (27,51,n) command in
the BASIC program.The reason for
doing this was to see if I could
get as good a printout of Outlet
files with the printer in Epson
mode as I do with the printer in
IBM mode.

When using TABLOID in IBM mode I
can get the printout to fit
comfortably on A4 sheets with a
top margin of just under 1" and
a bottom margin of approximately
3/4". The height of the char-
acters is approximately 2mm and
I get 9 lines to the inch.


However, when the printer is
switched to the Epson mode and
the code altered so that ESC 3 n
gives the same line feed, the
height of the characters is
approximately 2.5mm giving no
spacing between successive
lines. In fact, the height of
the characters is the same as
those produced by normal print-
ing.


In that part of the "Contents"
program which controls the print
options you have used E$; S0 and
E$; e0; CHR$ VAL "20". Will you
please explain what these
commands do as I cannot find the
values for S0 or e0?


Thanks for the tip on Masterfile
+3.I have used the subscript
option on the menu and although
it doesn't enable the 8 or 10
lines per inch options to work
it does give a better printout.
The other option which doesn't
work on my printer is Letter
quality but this is no great
loss.

I still haven't found where the
printer codes are in the
program. I have carried out the
usual search but haven't had any
success to date, so if anyone
can help me with this it would
be much appreciated.

           M. Atkins

Brian Cavers to M. Atkins

The TABLOID program itself was
not written using the BASIC
programming language. BASIC is
just not fast enough for some
applications.TABLOID was written
in a different programming
language called machine code.

Normally on the Spectrum,machine
code files are loaded separately
but we usually put them in BASIC
REM statements. OUTLET programs
often have six,eight,ten or more
code blocks which, if separate,
would take longer to load, use
more disc space and imagine try-
ing to resave the whole program
with 10 or more different files,
including all the code details!


The TABLOID machine code program
is in the line 9991 REM in the
CONTENTS BASIC.You cannot see it
when you LIST 9991 as BASIC just
cannot interpret it.

The command 'GO SUB 9991'in line
1605 causes the TABLOID code to
be copied from the REM to memory
starting at 65215.If you want to
see it, enter GO SUB 9991 then
SAVE "TABLOID"CODE 65215,600. If
you then load it into OUTSTART
(OUTLET 13)you can list the pro-
gram but, of course, unless you
understand machine code it will
not make any sense.

Mike Haine,who wrote the TABLOID
program,put the ESC 3 line space
printer codes within it.


Later, TABLOID was linked to the
CONTENTS BASIC and other printer
codes were added to the BASIC.

The TABLOID program is called by
the RANDOMIZE USR 65215 in line
1605 and the USR 64768 in 1610.
The BASIC 'USR' command is used
to start machine code programs.
After completion they return to
the BASIC statement immediately
following the USR statement. It
is the TABLOID code which does
the clever printing; the BASIC
parts you see at lines 1600 on
just support the code to get the
pages right etc.

I hope that clarifies why you
cannot see all the printer codes
in TABLOID.


It's interesting that the height
of the characters is greater in
Epson mode to IBM mode. I didn't
know that.We heard recently that
24-pin printers give higher
characters but I didn't realize
they varied with the mode! That
explains why the TABLOID
printout goes wrong anyway.

Have you yet tried my solution
that I gave? Add a line...


       1607 POKE 64817,18

                       ...to the
CONTENTS BASIC. I think that was
what cured it in my reply to
Brian Birkett in OUTLETTERS 68
and 69.


The printer code "S0" is super-
script and "e0" is tab setting.
The full codes are...

          SUPERSCRIPT

CODE:      27       83       0

or... CHR$ 27; CHR$ 83; CHR$ 0

or... CHR$ 27;CHR$ 83; CHR$ 48

or...     ESC      "S"       0

MY BASIC:  E$      "S0"

I have put the CHR$ 27 in E$.
Most Epson-compatible printers
will accept CHR$ 48 and 49 (in
some situations) instead of 0
and 1. Let me clarify...


The characters "0" and "1" that
print on your screen or printer
have the ASCII codes 48 and 49.
They are actually CHR$ 48 and
49. These are the actual numbers
that DISPLAY or PRINT as 0 and 1
on your screen or printer. They
should not be confused with CHR$
0 and 1 which are totally
different.

In BASIC, enter PRINT CHR$ 0 and
you will get a question mark on
the screen because CHR$ 0 cannot
be printed! CHR$ 0 does NOT
represent the PRINTABLE digit as
seen in text. However,as stated,
many printer codes accept the
printable digits "0" and "1" in
some situations instead of the
CHR$ 0 and 1. Clear as mud?


          TAB SETTING

      27      101       0      n

 CHR$ 27;CHR$ 101; CHR$ 0;CHR$ n

 CHR$ 27;CHR$ 101;CHR$ 48;CHR$ n

     ESC      "S"       0      n

      E$      "S0";      CHR$ 20

It's just easier in BASIC to put
LPRINT E$;"e0";CHR$ 20. There is
no printable equivalent of CHR$
20 but if the TAB setting wanted
was say 40 instead of 20 I could
use LPRINT E$;"e0(" because CHR$
40 is the left bracket character
"(". I try to avoid using CHR$
if I can!


I have not studied MASTERFILE +3
in any detail but the reason you
cannot find the printer code is
almost certainly for the same
reason as TABLOID - MASTERFILE
is written in machine code so it
may not have any printer codes
LPRINTED from BASIC.

I should have to spend a week or
two familiarising myself with it
and then another week hacking
the code and experimenting to
see if I could affect the print.

Just a brief look reveals what
seems to be a hidden code file
called "SPMF     Q" where Q is
the UDG and there is no full
stop in the name! It probably
will not resave properly even if
hacked!                    Brian

From Malcolm Goodman, LEEDS

Dear Brian/Ron,

With talk of a PC version of
OUTLET being bandied about,
perhaps someone (you?) can give
some guidance for non-PC users
(me!) on what we need to be
looking for in the event that we
move over. Maybe some terms
could be explained such as...


EXTENDED 386, CACHE RAM, EGA,
VGA, HERCULES, AT, XT

                     ...and also
any other commonly-used terms so
that,should we buy a PC,we don't
go blindly at it.


Perhaps some suggestions as to
what software(particularly BASIC
language) we should consider, as
well as any other relevant
advice so that if a PC OUTLET
does appear we do at least have
a fighting chance of reading and
contributing to it.

        In anticipation,

        Malcolm Goodman

Brian Cavers to Malcolm Goodman

The PC OUTLET looks virtually
certain,perhaps at the start of
the new year, the only question
is "will it be successful enough
to keep me from cardboard city?"
OK, here are a few pointers...

The XT is an early machine then
is the AT then 286, 386, 486 and
soon the 586 which will be named
"pentium" I think because Intel
who make the processor have had
difficulty in getting copyright
protection for numbers. As you
can no doubt guess, each is just
a more powerful machine centred
around an ever-more powerful
processor chip. Forget the early
ones,except as history, look for
a MINIMUM 286.

Get a 386 or 486 if you can
afford it. I have heard that the
386 has overtaken the 286 in
popularity and the price gap
between 286 and 386 is getting
narrower so try for a 386 if
possible.

Processor speed also effects
performance - shown as eg, 20Mhz
or 33Mhz etc - the higher is
faster but also more costly.

You will also see suffixes SX
and DX. I think this relates to
the bus and DX is more powerful
than SX but again, more costly!

Yet again, you may see "with
maths co-processor chip" - even
more power and even more money!


One other thing enhances speed
and that is a cache (pronounced
cash - and yes, it needs more
cash!).They come in two flavours
- memory and disc caches...

A memory cache is a section of
RAM that is extra fast. Some
chips are faster than average
but of course they cost more so
it would be very expensive to
have the whole of RAM made of
these fast chips. The cache is
say, 64K of this fast RAM with a
software utility which runs in
the background(interrupt-driven)
and puts the most frequently
accessed sections of the
currently running program in
this fast RAM, thus speeding it
up.


A disc cache is an area of RAM
used to store a copy of data you
have recently written to or read
from a disc.When a program tries
to get the data from the disc it
is sent from this RAM instead
and so speeds things up. Again,a
utility resident elsewhere in
memory keeps track of what is
where and controls all this.Many
PC programs tend to access discs
frequently, almost like extra
memory and so a disc cache can
make a big difference.

There is no way for a layman to
assess how all these factors may
affect performance in real terms
so you can only go for the best
you can afford but bear in mind
the following...


1. If you think you may be using
power-intensive software like a
spreadsheet, advanced drawing or
CAD program, heavy database and
so on then performance is much
more important - less important
if not.

2. The PC is so flexible that it
can be expanded LATER so you do
not necessarily need to get all
the bells and whistles early.

HERCULES, CGA, EGA, VGA SVGA are
all"graphic adaptors" and affect
the display you can expect. The
first three are early and more
limited - forget them. Treat VGA
as minimum - it includes all the
earlier ones WITHIN it as"screen
modes" so it is still compatible
with programs that need them.

The top two screen modes in VGA
give...
   320 by 200 in 256 colours
   640 by 480 in 16 colours
          ...each from a palette
of about a quarter of a million.
This means, for example, colour
0 is black by default, 1 is blue
and 7 is dull white just as they
are on the Spectrum BUT each can
be changed to any of a quarter
of a million colours although
only 256 or 16 can be shown on
the screen at any one time.

SVGA,SUPER VGA gives 256 colours
in 640 by 480 mode but this is
not supported by the standard
BASIC (more later). I also think
SVGA can do far more but I don't
know if it needs special soft or
hardware. Anybody else know?.

This leads us to the BASIC. If
you get MSDOS 5 or later it has
a copy of QBASIC built in and it
can be regarded as the standard.
The listing is not tokenised as
on the Spectrum - it is just a
text file and can load into a
wordprocessor or into another
BASIC language where it will run
quite happily so long as the
syntax is compatible. I have
written a routine to convert
Spectrum programs this way but
they are especially incompatible
regarding syntax but I got the
CARPET pattern-maker (OUTLET 10)
working with a bit of modificat-
ion (more on Spectrum programs
later). QBASIC is loaded from
disc but you can customise your
PC to boot it in on reset if you
want!

The BASIC itself is VERY fast
and has many powerful features
but it also has many very poor
features compared to a Spectrum
and SAM. Perhaps this deserves a
complete article in itself in a
DRIVECHAT or something to give a
better idea. Suffice to say that
overall I have thoroughly got
into the swing of it and really
enjoy using it. It takes time to
fathom it all out though because
the provided (on-screen) manual
is poor and many things we take
for granted on the Spectrum are
quite different. However, I did
manage to get an excellent book,
THE "QUICK BASIC BIBLE" (Waite
Group - Microsoft Press - Waite,
Arnson, Gemmell and Henderson,
ISBN 1-55615-262-0 `27.95) and
this opened it up for me.

Of course,the new PC OUTLET will
feature articles and programs
for QUICK BASIC as well as help
and advice.

I mentioned QBASIC which comes
"free" with MS DOS but no hard
copy of the manual. It is really
a version of QUICK BASIC with
some features omitted but it can
still run all QUICK BASIC prog-
rams.The main difference is that
QUICK BASIC comes with a built-
in compiler - you just click on
a menu option. As provided, the
BASIC programs can't run without
the BASIC editor environment-you
have to load BASIC first and
then a BASIC program into it.You
can do it with one DOS command
to load QB plus a BASIC program
but the user must have BASIC.

To produce stand-alone programs
that run from DOS you need the
compiler. I was unable to get
this on its own for use with
QBASIC and finished up getting a
new copy of QUICK BASIC with the
compiler.I'm still not convinced
that this was absolutely necess-
ary and it may be possible to
purchase the compiler alone but
I couldn't find it anywhere.

I have not done any specific
time tests yet but I get the
impression that compiled BASIC
is not essentially any FASTER. I
suspect that it simply produces
a stand-alone file that will run
on any PC without BASIC. I think
the reason why it may not be any
faster is as follows...(wait for
it!)...

Crazy as it sounds, I get the
impression that even in the
BASIC editor environment, when
you RUN the program,it is really
very rapidly compiled and run as
code! In other words, it may not
be translated AS IT RUNS like on
the Spectrum(and all other comp-
uters that I know of) but pre-
translated.The separate compiler
is probably just to organize the
supporting routines etc. and
produce a stand-alone program.

This is all guesswork but that's
what I suspect!

Anyway, to sum up, the BASIC is
fine and so long as you get a
machine with MS DOS 5 or later
you have it included "free".


Next, the drives. You CAN run a
PC with just a floppy drive but
I would only regard that as a
stepping-stone economy measure
until you can afford a hard
drive. I don't know why one of
the big manufacturers doesn't
produce a cut-price PC with just
a floppy and a tv modulator for
around `250 - it ought to be
possible. However, it must be
fully expandable - not like the
Amstrad effort from a few years
back.

However, in all seriousness, few
would consider extensive use
without a hard drive. Get a min-
imum of 40mb - this is regarded
as small these days! Get bigger
if you can afford it.


There is a utility named STACKER
which virtually doubles the
storage of a hard drive using a
different method of writing. It
is a well-proven and very popu-
lar program and worth consider-
ing although it is not cheap.
MS DOS 6 and onwards INCLUDES a
similar compressor but there
have been doubts about its
reliability. How anyone can use
such an important thing as a DOS
if there even a shadow of susp-
icion about it I don't know!

You must have a floppy drive as
well as a hard disc else you
can't get any new software! The
high density are now standard
giving about 1.5mb after format
but you could manage with a
double-density one.

You should also get a mouse.They
are relatively cheap for the PC
and a lot of software uses them.

You are probably looking at say,
`700 for a reasonable but modest
386 33mhz machine with SVGA and
40mb hard drive plus floppy,
mouse, DOS and probably lots of
odds and ends of software.

Software comes in two extremes:
there is a huge amount of very
inexpensive public domain and
shareware (although quite a bit
of shareware needs `20 to `50 to
register!) but at the other end,
much commercial software is very
expensive - the leading art and
graphic drawing programs are in
the `300 to `400 range upwards!


Shareware is a type of PD which
is often a cut-down or demo
version. You are supposed to try
it for a period then erase it.If
you like it and want to continue
using it you pay a "registration
fee" to get the full version.

I must also mention WINDOWS. It
is a WIMP desktop utility from
Microsoft that is becoming the
standard replacement for direct
DOS (of course DOS still runs
"underneath"it).It is far better
than the ST desktop but is very
slow to boot in and uses a hell
of a lot of disc space and RAM.
You may find it included with a
new PC package. I am more than
happy to use XTREE which is an
easy-to-use file handler and
loader.

PC's usually come with a minimum
of 1mb of memory and this seems
to be roughly as follows...


   0 to around 2K(?) BIOS and
                     sysvars etc

2000 to 640K  running program(s)

640K to 768K  screen memory

768K to 832K  "expanded" memory
               paged in here in
               64K blocks

832K to 896K   ???
896K to 1000K  ROM (but suspect
               it is copied to
               RAM at same addr-
               esses for speed?


You can add extra RAM in 1mbs,
either paged in 64K chunks to
address 768K or accessed above
1mb as "extended" memory.I won't
go into details but it's all the
same memory;it is how the system
is set up and RAM allocated that
gives it the names. If paged in
at 768K it is called "expanded"
and if accessed above 1mb it is
"extended". I think it needs a
386 or greater to use "extended"
memory. There is also a term
"high" memory which is a 64K
extension above a 1mb DOS window
because the processor can only
look at 64K windows within the
640K window that DOS can use but
the last 64K window starts just
below the end and therefore
overlaps! Geddit?


There is much about the memory I
have yet to understand but, in
use, the system handles it. On a
PC you just load a file and the
system decides where it will go,
keeps a note and prevents any-
thing else going there and
frees it when finished. The user
generally need not worry about
memory unless you get a message
saying you've too many programs
in memory at once - remove some!

Finally, I must mention the Z80
Lunter Spectrum emulator from BG
SERVICES which runs Spectrum
programs. A future version may
run your +D OUTLET discs direct!
(see Brian Gaff's letter). It
really is excellent.
                           Brian

Brian Cavers to M. Atkins

The TABLOID program itself was not written using the BASIC programming language. BASIC is just not fast enough for some applications.TABLOID was written in a different programming language called machine code.

Normally on the Spectrum,machine code files are loaded separately but we usually put them in BASIC REM statements. OUTLET programs often have six,eight,ten or more code blocks which, if separate, would take longer to load, use more disc space and imagine try- ing to resave the whole program with 10 or more different files, including all the code details!

The TABLOID machine code program is in the line 9991 REM in the CONTENTS BASIC.You cannot see it when you LIST 9991 as BASIC just cannot interpret it.

The command 'GO SUB 9991'in line 1605 causes the TABLOID code to be copied from the REM to memory starting at 65215.If you want to see it, enter GO SUB 9991 then SAVE "TABLOID"CODE 65215,600. If you then load it into OUTSTART (OUTLET 13)you can list the pro- gram but, of course, unless you understand machine code it will not make any sense.

Mike Haine,who wrote the TABLOID program,put the ESC 3 line space printer codes within it.

Later, TABLOID was linked to the CONTENTS BASIC and other printer codes were added to the BASIC.

The TABLOID program is called by the RANDOMIZE USR 65215 in line 1605 and the USR 64768 in 1610. The BASIC 'USR' command is used to start machine code programs. After completion they return to the BASIC statement immediately following the USR statement. It is the TABLOID code which does the clever printing; the BASIC parts you see at lines 1600 on just support the code to get the pages right etc.

I hope that clarifies why you cannot see all the printer codes in TABLOID.

It's interesting that the height of the characters is greater in Epson mode to IBM mode. I didn't know that.We heard recently that 24-pin printers give higher characters but I didn't realize they varied with the mode! That explains why the TABLOID printout goes wrong anyway.

The characters "0" and "1" that print on your screen or printer have the ASCII codes 48 and 49. They are actually CHR$ 48 and 49. These are the actual numbers that DISPLAY or PRINT as 0 and 1 on your screen or printer. They should not be confused with CHR$ 0 and 1 which are totally different.

In BASIC, enter PRINT CHR$ 0 and you will get a question mark on the screen because CHR$ 0 cannot be printed! CHR$ 0 does NOT represent the PRINTABLE digit as seen in text. From Malcolm Goodman, LEEDS

Dear Brian/Ron,

With talk of a PC version of OUTLET being bandied about, perhaps someone (you?) can give some guidance for non-PC users (me!) on what we need to be looking for in the event that we move over. Maybe some terms could be explained such as...

EXTENDED 386, CACHE RAM, EGA, VGA, HERCULES, AT, XT

...and also any other commonly-used terms so that,should we buy a PC,we don't go blindly at it.

Brian Cavers to Malcolm Goodman

The PC OUTLET looks virtually certain,perhaps at the start of the new year, the only question is "will it be successful enough to keep me from cardboard city?" OK, here are a few pointers...

The XT is an early machine then is the AT then 286, 386, 486 and soon the 586 which will be named "pentium" I think because Intel who make the processor have had difficulty in getting copyright protection for numbers. As you can no doubt guess, each is just a more powerful machine centred around an ever-more powerful processor chip. Forget the early ones,except as history, look for a MINIMUM 286.

Get a 386 or 486 if you can afford it. I have heard that the 386 has overtaken the 286 in popularity and the price gap between 286 and 386 is getting narrower so try for a 386 if possible.

Processor speed also effects performance - shown as eg, 20Mhz or 33Mhz etc - the higher is faster but also more costly.

You will also see suffixes SX and DX. I think this relates to the bus and DX is more powerful than SX but again, more costly!

Yet again, you may see "with maths co-processor chip" - even more power and even more money!

One other thing enhances speed and that is a cache (pronounced cash - and yes, it needs more cash!).They come in two flavours - memory and disc caches...

A memory cache is a section of RAM that is extra fast. Some chips are faster than average but of course they cost more so it would be very expensive to have the whole of RAM made of these fast chips. The cache is say, 64K of this fast RAM with a software utility which runs in the background(interrupt-driven) and puts the most frequently accessed sections of the currently running program in this fast RAM, thus speeding it up.

A disc cache is an area of RAM used to store a copy of data you have recently written to or read from a disc.When a program tries to get the data from the disc it is sent from this RAM instead and so speeds things up. Again,a utility resident elsewhere in memory keeps track of what is where and controls all this.Many PC programs tend to access discs frequently, almost like extra memory and so a disc cache can make a big difference.

There is no way for a layman to assess how all these factors may affect performance in real terms so you can only go for the best you can afford but bear in mind the following...

1. If you think you may be using power-intensive software like a spreadsheet, advanced drawing or CAD program, heavy database and so on then performance is much more important - less important if not.

2. The PC is so flexible that it can be expanded LATER so you do not necessarily need to get all the bells and whistles early.

HERCULES, CGA, EGA, VGA SVGA are all"graphic adaptors" and affect the display you can expect. The first three are early and more limited - forget them. Treat VGA as minimum - it includes all the earlier ones WITHIN it as"screen modes" so it is still compatible with programs that need them.

The top two screen modes in VGA give... 320 by 200 in 256 colours 640 by 480 in 16 colours ...each from a palette of about a quarter of a million. This means, for example, colour 0 is black by default, 1 is blue and 7 is dull white just as they are on the Spectrum BUT each can be changed to any of a quarter of a million colours although only 256 or 16 can be shown on the screen at any one time.

SVGA,SUPER VGA gives 256 colours in 640 by 480 mode but this is not supported by the standard BASIC (more later). I also think SVGA can do far more but I don't know if it needs special soft or hardware. Anybody else know?.

This leads us to the BASIC. If you get MSDOS 5 or later it has a copy of QBASIC built in and it can be regarded as the standard. The listing is not tokenised as on the Spectrum - it is just a text file and can load into a wordprocessor or into another BASIC language where it will run quite happily so long as the syntax is compatible. I have written a routine to convert Spectrum programs this way but they are especially incompatible regarding syntax but I got the CARPET pattern-maker (OUTLET 10) working with a bit of modificat- ion (more on Spectrum programs later). QBASIC is loaded from disc but you can customise your PC to boot it in on reset if you want!

The BASIC itself is VERY fast and has many powerful features but it also has many very poor features compared to a Spectrum and SAM. Perhaps this deserves a complete article in itself in a DRIVECHAT or something to give a better idea. Suffice to say that overall I have thoroughly got into the swing of it and really enjoy using it. It takes time to fathom it all out though because the provided (on-screen) manual is poor and many things we take for granted on the Spectrum are quite different. However, I did manage to get an excellent book, THE "QUICK BASIC BIBLE" (Waite Group - Microsoft Press - Waite, Arnson, Gemmell and Henderson, ISBN 1-55615-262-0 `27.95) and this opened it up for me.

Of course,the new PC OUTLET will feature articles and programs for QUICK BASIC as well as help and advice.

I mentioned QBASIC which comes "free" with MS DOS but no hard copy of the manual. It is really a version of QUICK BASIC with some features omitted but it can still run all QUICK BASIC prog- rams.The main difference is that QUICK BASIC comes with a built- in compiler - you just click on a menu option. As provided, the BASIC programs can't run without the BASIC editor environment-you have to load BASIC first and then a BASIC program into it.You can do it with one DOS command to load QB plus a BASIC program but the user must have BASIC.

To produce stand-alone programs that run from DOS you need the compiler. I was unable to get this on its own for use with QBASIC and finished up getting a new copy of QUICK BASIC with the compiler.I'm still not convinced that this was absolutely necess- ary and it may be possible to purchase the compiler alone but I couldn't find it anywhere.

I have not done any specific time tests yet but I get the impression that compiled BASIC is not essentially any FASTER. I suspect that it simply produces a stand-alone file that will run on any PC without BASIC. I think the reason why it may not be any faster is as follows...(wait for it!)...

Crazy as it sounds, I get the impression that even in the BASIC editor environment, when you RUN the program,it is really very rapidly compiled and run as code! In other words, it may not be translated AS IT RUNS like on the Spectrum(and all other comp- uters that I know of) but pre- translated.The separate compiler is probably just to organize the supporting routines etc. and produce a stand-alone program.

This is all guesswork but that's what I suspect!

Anyway, to sum up, the BASIC is fine and so long as you get a machine with MS DOS 5 or later you have it included "free".

Next, the drives. You CAN run a PC with just a floppy drive but I would only regard that as a stepping-stone economy measure until you can afford a hard drive. I don't know why one of the big manufacturers doesn't produce a cut-price PC with just a floppy and a tv modulator for around `250 - it ought to be possible. However, it must be fully expandable - not like the Amstrad effort from a few years back.

However, in all seriousness, few would consider extensive use without a hard drive. Get a min- imum of 40mb - this is regarded as small these days! Get bigger if you can afford it.

There is a utility named STACKER which virtually doubles the storage of a hard drive using a different method of writing. It is a well-proven and very popu- lar program and worth consider- ing although it is not cheap. MS DOS 6 and onwards INCLUDES a similar compressor but there have been doubts about its reliability. How anyone can use such an important thing as a DOS if there even a shadow of susp- icion about it I don't know!

You must have a floppy drive as well as a hard disc else you can't get any new software! The high density are now standard giving about 1.5mb after format but you could manage with a double-density one.

You should also get a mouse.They are relatively cheap for the PC and a lot of software uses them.

You are probably looking at say, `700 for a reasonable but modest 386 33mhz machine with SVGA and 40mb hard drive plus floppy, mouse, DOS and probably lots of odds and ends of software.

Software comes in two extremes: there is a huge amount of very inexpensive public domain and shareware (although quite a bit of shareware needs `20 to `50 to register!) but at the other end, much commercial software is very expensive - the leading art and graphic drawing programs are in the `300 to `400 range upwards!

Shareware is a type of PD which is often a cut-down or demo version. You are supposed to try it for a period then erase it.If you like it and want to continue using it you pay a "registration fee" to get the full version.

I must also mention WINDOWS. It is a WIMP desktop utility from Microsoft that is becoming the standard replacement for direct DOS (of course DOS still runs "underneath"it).It is far better than the ST desktop but is very slow to boot in and uses a hell of a lot of disc space and RAM. You may find it included with a new PC package. I am more than happy to use XTREE which is an easy-to-use file handler and loader.

PC's usually come with a minimum of 1mb of memory and this seems to be roughly as follows...

0 to around 2K(?) BIOS and sysvars etc

2000 to 640K  running program(s)

Сама программа TABLOID была написана не на языке программирования BASIC. Для некоторых задач BASIC просто недостаточно быстр. TABLOID был написан на другом языке — в машинных кодах.

Обычно на Spectrum файлы машинного кода загружаются отдельно, но мы, как правило, помещаем их в строки REM языка BASIC. Программы в OUTLET часто содержат шесть, восемь, десять или более блоков кода. Если бы они были отдельными, они загружались бы дольше, занимали больше места на диске, да и представьте себе попытку пересохранить всю программу с 10 и более разными файлами, включая все адреса и параметры кода!

Машинный код TABLOID находится в строке 9991 REM бейсиковской программы CONTENTS. Вы не увидите его, набрав `LIST 9991`, потому что BASIC просто не способен его интерпретировать.

Команда `GO SUB 9991` в строке 1605 копирует код TABLOID из строки REM в память, начиная с адреса 65215. Если хотите взглянуть на него, введите `GO SUB 9991`, а затем `SAVE "TABLOID"CODE 65215,600`. Если затем загрузить его в OUTSTART (OUTLET 13), вы сможете получить листинг программы, но, конечно, если вы не разбираетесь в машинном коде, он покажется вам бессмыслицей.

Mike Haine, написавший программу TABLOID, поместил команды управления межстрочным интервалом ESC 3 прямо внутри неё.

Позже TABLOID связали с программой CONTENTS на BASIC, и остальные коды принтера были добавлены уже в BASIC.

Программа TABLOID вызывается командами `RANDOMIZE USR 65215` в строке 1605 и `USR 64768` в строке 1610. Команда BASIC `USR` используется для запуска программ в машинном коде. После завершения они возвращают управление в оператор BASIC, следующий сразу за оператором USR. Именно машинный код TABLOID выполняет всю хитрую печать; части на BASIC, которые вы видите начиная со строки 1600, лишь помогают коду правильно разбивать текст на страницы и т.д.

Выход PC OUTLET кажется практически решённым делом, возможно, в начале нового года; единственный вопрос — «будет ли он достаточно успешным, чтобы спасти меня от жизни в картонной коробке на улице?» Что ж, вот несколько ориентиров...

XT — это старая машина, затем идёт AT, затем 286, 386, 486 и вскоре 586, который, кажется, назовут «pentium», потому что у Intel, производящей эти процессоры, возникли трудности с защитой авторских прав на числа. Как вы, несомненно, догадались, каждый следующий компьютер просто мощнее предыдущего и построен вокруг ещё более производительного чипа процессора. Забудьте о ранних моделях, оставив их истории, и ориентируйтесь как МИНИМУМ на 286.

Берите 386 или 486, если позволяют средства. Я слышал, что 386 обогнал 286 по популярности, а ценовой разрыв между 286 и 386 сокращается, поэтому по возможности нацеливайтесь на 386.

Скорость процессора также влияет на производительность — она указывается, например, как 20 МГц или 33 МГц и т.д. Чем выше частота, тем быстрее компьютер, но и дороже.

Вы также увидите суффиксы SX и DX. Полагаю, это связано с шиной данных, и DX мощнее, чем SX, но опять же — дороже!

И ещё вы можете встретить приписку «с математическим сопроцессором» — ещё больше мощи и ещё больше денег!

Еще одна вещь, повышающая скорость работы — это кэш (cache, произносится как «кэш» — и да, на него требуется больше наличных/cash!). Они бывают двух видов — кэш памяти и дисковый кэш...

Кэш памяти — это область сверхбыстрой оперативной памяти (RAM). Некоторые микросхемы работают быстрее среднего уровня, но, разумеется, стоят дороже, поэтому делать всю память из таких чипов вышло бы невероятно накладно. Кэш — это, скажем, 64 Кб такой быстрой RAM в связке с программной утилитой, которая работает в фоновом режиме (по прерываниям) и помещает наиболее часто используемые участки текущей программы в эту скоростную память, тем самым ускоряя её работу.

Дисковый кэш — это область обычной RAM, используемая для хранения копии данных, которые вы недавно записали на диск или считали с него. Когда программа пытается получить данные с диска, они считываются из этой оперативной памяти, что значительно всё ускоряет. Опять же, резидентная утилита, находящаяся в памяти, отслеживает, где что лежит, и управляет процессом. Многие программы для PC имеют свойство обращаться к дискам постоянно, используя их чуть ли не как дополнительную память, поэтому дисковый кэш дает огромный прирост.

Неспециалисту невозможно оценить, как все эти факторы скажутся на производительности на практике, поэтому берите лучшее из того, что можете себе позволить, но имейте в виду следующее...

1. Если вы планируете работать с ресурсоемким софтом — электронными таблицами, продвинутыми графическими редакторами или CAD-системами, тяжелыми базами данных и т. д., то производительность крайне важна; если нет — она менее критична.

2. PC настолько гибок, что его можно проапгрейдить ПОЗЖЕ, так что вам вовсе не обязательно сразу покупать все навороты.

HERCULES, CGA, EGA, VGA, SVGA — все это «графические адаптеры», определяющие возможности вывода на экран. Первые три — старые и весьма ограниченные, забудьте о них. VGA считайте минимумом — он включает в себя все предыдущие стандарты ВНУТРИ себя как «видеорежимы», так что сохраняет полную совместимость с программами, требующими старых карт.

Два топовых режима в VGA дают:
* 320 на 200 при 256 цветах
* 640 на 480 при 16 цветах
...каждый выбирается из палитры примерно в четверть миллиона цветов. Это означает, например, что цвет 0 по умолчанию черный, 1 — синий, а 7 — тускло-белый, точно как на Spectrum, НО каждый цвет можно переназначить на любой из четверти миллиона оттенков, хотя одновременно на экране может отображаться только 256 или 16.

SVGA (SUPER VGA) дает 256 цветов в режиме 640 на 480, но это не поддерживается стандартным BASIC (подробнее об этом ниже). Я также слышал, что SVGA способна на гораздо большее, но не знаю, требует ли это специального софта или «железа». Может, кто-нибудь в курсе?
